case_name: Cicada Ventures Ltd. v. KGHM Ajax Mining Inc.
text:
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA

Citation:

Cicada Ventures Ltd. v. KGHM Ajax
Mining Inc.,

2016 BCSC 1677

Date: 20160912

Docket:
52937

Registry: Kamloops

Between:

Cicada Ventures Ltd.

Plaintiff

And

KGHM Ajax Mining Inc.

Defendant

Before: Master R.W. McDiarmid

Reasons for Judgment

Counsel for the Plaintiff:

J.
Frame

Counsel for the Defendant:

R.W.
Millen

Place and Date of Hearing:

Kamloops,
B.C.

August
29, 2016

Place and Date of Judgment:

Kamloops,
B.C.

September
12, 2016

[
1
]

By notice of application filed July 21, 2016,
the defendant sought five orders as follows:

1.         An Order that the Plaintiff,
Cicada Ventures Ltd. post security for the costs of this proceeding in the amount
of $62,352 within thirty (30) days of the date of this Order, or such other
amount as is determined by this Honourable Court.

2.         An Order that the Plaintiff
respond to the Defendant’s demand for particulars dated June 15, 2016 within
three (3) business days of the date of this Order.

3.         An Order that this action be
stayed until such time as the Plaintiff posts security for the costs of this
proceeding and responds to the demand for particulars dated June 15, 2016.

4.         An Order that this action be dismissed
as abandoned without further Order of this Court if the Plaintiff fails to post
the security and provide a response to the demand for particulars ordered by
this Court within thirty (30) days of the date of this Order.

5.         An
Order that the Plaintiff pay the costs of this application, in any event of the
cause.

[
2
]

At the commencement of the hearing, I was
advised that the order sought in paragraph 2, that the plaintiff respond to the
defendant’s demand for particulars was no longer in issue. Particulars had been
provided and were included in the chambers record binder.

[
3
]

By way of background, on May 13, 2016, the
plaintiff filed a notice of civil claim seeking damages and injunctive relief
against the defendant. On June 16, 2016, the defendant filed a response to the
civil claim. No other steps have been taken in this action other than a demand
for particulars, and provision of the particulars.

[
4
]

In its “FACTUAL BASIS”, paragraphs 7-17, the
defendant applicant sets out its overview of the claim and KGHM’s response as
follows:

7.         Cicada’s claim against KGHM
arises out of KGHM’s development of the Ajax Project. The Ajax Project is
proposed to consist of a 23-year open-pit mine (the “
Mine
”) and a number
of mine facilities (the “
Mine Facilities
”).

8.         KGHM has proposed to locate some
of the Mine Facilities on land owned by KGHM (the “
Lands
”) with respect
to which KGHM does not own the subsurface mineral rights.

9.         Cicada alleges that it is the
beneficial owner of certain mineral claims below the Lands as well as certain
additional mineral tenure claims (collectively the “
Iron Mask Mineral Claims
”).
It appears that at all material times prior to September 2014, an individual
named Laurence Sookochoff was the registered owner of the Iron Mask Mineral
Claims.

Notice of Civil Claim, paras. 3-4

10.       KGHM wished to conduct certain
work in or around the Iron Mask Mineral Claims in connection with the
development of the Mine. This included drilling and testing to determine
whether the proposed location of the Mine Facilities had appropriate surface
and geological stability to support the Mine Facilities (“
Geotechical
Drilling
”). In addition, KGHM wished to conduct drilling and testing to
demonstrate that the proposed location of the Mine Facilities did not contain
economic mineralization, such that developing the surface above the Iron Mask
Mineral Claims would not interfere with profitable development of those claims
(“
Condemnation Drilling
”).

Response to Civil Claim, paras. 6-12

11.       Cicada pleads that in December
2013, Cicada and KGHM entered into an agreement whereby KGHM would purchase the
Iron Mask Mineral Claim from Cicada and Mr. Sookochoff.

Notice of Civil Claim, para. 5

12.       In its Response to Civil Claim,
KGHM denies that it entered into any agreement with Cicada. The parties (KGHM,
Cicada and, at times, Mr. Sookochoff) never came to a meeting of the minds on
the material terms of any proposed agreement for the purchase and sale of the
Iron Mask Mineral Claims. Rather, they exchanged various offers with different
prices and for different mineral claims over several years. It is telling that
there is no executed agreement between or among the parties for the sale of the
Iron Mask Mineral Claims.

13.       Alternatively, even if KGHM and
Cicada entered into an agreement, such an agreement was repudiated or abandoned
by Cicada. Cicada also failed to perform a number of conditions precedent to
engage KGHM’s obligations under any purported agreement.

14.       Cicada also pleads that in October
2014, KGHM entered upon some or all of the Iron Mask Mineral Claims without its
permission and conducted mineral exploration. Cicada claims that KGHM’s
drilling was unlawful and that the permits under which KGHM conducted the
drilling were and remain “invalid”.

Notice of Civil Claim, paras. 7-11

15.       Cicada seeks damages for breach of
contract, trespass to chattels, conversion, interference with economic
relations, and unjust enrichment.

16.       In response, KGHM pleads,
inter
alia
, that:

(a)        KGHM conducted
both the Geotechnical Drilling and the Condemnation Drilling in accordance with
permits received from the Ministry of Mines and Energy (the “
Ministry
”)
and consistent with standard geological testing practices;

(b)        KGHM did not
need permission to conduct Geotechnical Drilling on the Iron Mask Mineral
Claims;

(c)        KGHM was
authorized by the Ministry to conduct the Condemnation Drilling without
Cicada’s permission;

(d)        Cicada’s
challenge to the Ministry permits is an unlawful collateral attack; and

(e)        KGHM complied
with its permit, has provided Cicada the results of its Condemnation Drilling
in a report dated May 2015 (the “
Condemnation Drilling Report
”), and has
offered to provide all mineral cores to Cicada.

Response to Civil Claim,
paras. 24-39.

17.       The
Condemnation Drilling Report concluded that the Iron Mask Mineral Claims did
not demonstrate “any significant mineralization”.

[
5
]

The plaintiff does not contest that it has no
present ability to pay costs. It is a public company whose shares are listed
and traded on the TSX Venture Exchange. This requires filing quarterly and
annual financial statements and other documents setting out the plaintiff’s
financial status. Those documents confirm:

(a)        Cicada has not
reported any revenue for the last three fiscal years.

(b)        Cicada “does
not have any source of revenue, except for the interest on cash deposits.
Cicada uses equity financing and advances from related parties to support its
operations.”

(c)        Cicada has
posted net losses of $361,519 in 2016, $307,477 in 2015, and $347,233 in 2014.
Cicada has posted losses in the eight most recent quarters.

(d)        Cicada has
$255 in cash on hand and current assets of $8,279.

(e)        Cicada has
current liabilities of $1,066,606 (up from $596,781 in 2015), and a working
capital deficit of $952,632. Cicada reports that the “increase in total
liabilities is due to the lack of sufficient cash flow available within the
Company to repay outstanding obligations as they become due.”

(f)        Cicada owes $44,310
in administration fees as of January 2016 and, as of April 30, 2016, owes its
directors $24,750.

[
6
]

In its condensed interim financial statements
(unaudited) for the three months and, at April 30, 2016, appended to an
affidavit of Donna Barnes, a legal administrative assistant for defendant’s
counsel, there is written the following:

a) Going Concern of Operations

The Company has not generated revenue from
operations. The Company incurred a net loss of $100,095 during the three months
ended April 30, 2016 (2015: $80,786) and as of that date the Company’s deficit
was $8,808,230 (2015: $8,427,402). The Company expects to incur further losses
in the development of its business, all of which casts significant doubt about
the Company’s ability to continue as a going concern. The Company’s ability to
continue as a going concern is dependent upon its ability to raise the
necessary funds and/or to obtain the necessary financing to meet its
obligations and repay its liabilities arising from normal business operations
when they come due. Although the Company has successfully raised funds in the
past, there is no assurance that it will be able to do so in the future.

[
7
]

The plaintiff filed a response, but no affidavit
material. It concedes the correctness of its financial situation as alleged by
the applicant.

[
8
]

What makes the situation less clear, though, is
contained in the response to demand for particulars. That response attaches two
documents. Both documents are entitled “Mineral Property Purchase Agreement”.
One of the documents, Schedule A to the response to demand for particulars, is
dated for reference December 30, 2013. Schedule B is a similar document dated
for reference March 4, 2014.

[
9
]

Both documents define “property” as ten mineral
claims described in a schedule which forms part of the document. Both documents
reference the plaintiff agreeing to sell to the defendant and the defendant
agreeing to purchase from the plaintiff 100% interest in and to the property,
defined as the “Purchased Interest” subject to a 20% net profit interest
royalty in favour of the plaintiff.

[
10
]

The December 30, 2013 document, at paragraph
2.2, states “The purchase price for the Purchased Interest shall be the amount
of $1,000,000 in cash …” That document was signed by the defendant and one of
the parties to the document, who, according to the document, holds the property
in trust for the benefit of the plaintiff. It was not signed by the plaintiff.

[
11
]

The March 4, 2014 document, at paragraph 2.2,
states “The purchase price for the Purchased Interest shall be the amount of
$1,350,000…” It goes on to state that $1,000,000 is paid to the plaintiff and
$350,000 to Mr. Sookochoff. That document was not signed by any of the parties.

[
12
]

According to the defendant’s response to the
notice of civil claim, the March 4, 2014 document was prepared by the
defendant. Paragraph 15 of the response to civil claim is as follows:

15.       Following
Cicada and Mr. Sookochoff’s rejection of the December 2013 Offer, in or about
March 2014 KGHM tendered a further offer to Cicada and Mr. Sookochoff to
purchase the Iron Mask Mineral Claims for $1,350,000 (the “
March 2014 Offer
”).

[
13
]

Paragraph 18 of the response to civil claim sets
out the history of the offers from its perspective. I am aware that these are
pleadings and not proven facts. They are instructive in properly appreciating
the plaintiff’s submissions. Paragraph 18 is as follows:

18.       Between November 2014 and April
2016, Cicada and KGHM exchanged a number of offers and counteroffers for the
purchase and sale of part or all of the Iron Mask Mineral Claims, particulars
of which are as follows:

(a)        On
or about November 3, 2014, having resolved its dispute with Mr. Sookochoff,
Cicada rejected the March 2014 Offer and demanded $5,000,000 for the Iron Mask
Mineral Claims.

(b)        On
or about November 6, 2014, KGHM responded by renewing the December 2013 Offer.

(c)        On
or about December 19, 2014, KGHM provided a revised draft written agreement
with Mr. Sookochoff no longer a party, and an offer to purchase the Iron Mask
Mineral Claims for $1,000,000.

(d)        On
or about April 23, 2015, Cicada responded to KGHM’s December 19, 2014 offer by
offering to sell the Iron Mask Mineral Claims for $1,700,000.

(e)        On
or about May 11, 2015, KGHM sent a letter to Cicada that included an offer of
$750,000 for the Iron Mask Mineral Claims.

(f)        On
or about May 14, 2015, Cicada sent KGHM an email offering to sell the Iron Mask
Mineral Claims on certain terms.

(g)        On
or about May 20, 2015, KGHM sent Cicada a revised draft written agreement with
an offer to purchase the Iron Mask Mineral Claims on specified terms.

(h)        On
or about June 30, 2015, Cicada advised KGHM that it rejected the most recent
draft written agreement.

(i)         On
or about October 9, 2015, Cicada emailed KGHM an offer to sell only a portion
of the Iron Mask Mineral Claims for $1,100,000.

(j)         On
or about October 27, 2015, KGHM emailed Cicada an offer to purchase the Iron
Mask Mineral Claims for $200,000.

(k)        On
or about March 14, 2016, Cicada sent a letter to KGHM purporting to accept the
December 2013 Offer, and enclosing a revised copy of the draft agreement that
had been sent by KGHM as part of its March 2014 Offer.

(l)         On or about
April 11, 2016, KGHM wrote to Cicada offering to purchase a portion of the Iron
Mask Mineral Claims for $200,000.

[
14
]

Christopher Wild, the project manager for the
defendant, was, until May 30, 2016, chief geologist for the defendant’s project
to develop the proposed Ajax Mine. He oversaw drilling condemnation operations
within the mineral claims he understood were owned by the plaintiff. In May
2015, he drafted a report setting out his conclusions on the economic
mineralization found within the mineral claims. He attached a copy of his
report which succinctly summarized the purpose of condemnation drilling in the
conclusion section as follows:

The British
Columbia Ministry of Energy and Mines (BCMEM) requires that condemnation
drilling be undertaken to assess the ground under which permanent mine
facilities are proposed to ensure that mineral resources will not be
sterilized. The East and South Mine Rock Storage Facilities are situated on (or
adjacent to) mineral claims owned by Cicada Ventures Ltd. (“Cicada”).

[
15
]

The third paragraph of the conclusions contained
the following:

The Ajax south
footprint is largely underlain by volcanic, volcaniclastic, and related
sedimentary rocks of the Upper Triassic Nicola Group. The Nicola Group rocks
are generally not prospective for bulk tonnage porphyry copper - gold deposits.
Condemnation and geotechnical drilling confirmed both the presence of Nicola
volcanic rocks and the lack of significant copper-gold mineralization in those
rocks underlying the Ajax south footprint.

[
16
]

The last three paragraphs under the conclusions
are as follows:

The Plant Site, Conveyor, and Crusher area
straddles the contact between the Nicola Group to the south and intrusive rocks
of the Iron Mask Batholith to the north. No significant economic mineralization
was encountered in the area.

Drilling in the EMRSF footprint intersected
Cherry Creek Monzonite, Sugarloaf Diorite (SLD), and Iron Mask Hybrid (IMH). No
significant mineralization was encountered.

Condemnation and
geotechnical drilling completed in 2014 and the first quarter of 2015 was
successful in condemning the entire southern footprint.

[
17
]

The gist of the plaintiff’s case is that the
conducting of the condemnation drilling was tortious and, by conducting that
drilling and determining that there was no economic mineralization, the
defendant essentially destroyed the value of the plaintiff’s asset.

[
18
]

Plaintiff’s counsel, in his submissions, made
the analogy to an intact “Scratch and Win” lottery ticket’s economic value;
once it is scratched and there is a determination that it is not a “winner”, it
has no value.

[
19
]

In essence, the plaintiff says that it is the
defendant’s own tortious conduct, or alternatively its conduct in breaching
contractual obligations, that has put the plaintiff in a position where it is
unable to pay costs if it is unsuccessful in the litigation.

APPLICABLE LAW

[
20
]

The starting point is
s. 236
of the
Business
Corporations Act
, S.B.C. 2002, c. 57, which is as follows:

236
If a corporation is the plaintiff in a legal proceeding brought
before the court, and if it appears that the corporation will be unable to pay
the costs of the defendant if the defendant is successful in the defence, the
court may require security to be given by the corporation for those costs, and
may stay all legal proceedings until the security is given.

[
21
]

The notice of application in Part 3, Legal
Basis, paragraph 3, sets out that the court has inherent jurisdiction to order
a party to post security for costs; only a judge of the court has inherent
jurisdiction. A master’s jurisdiction is statutory, based on s. 236.

[
22
]

In
Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform Inc. v.
Canadian Jewish Congress
,
1999 CanLII 5860 (BC SC)
, [1999] B.C.J. No. 2160, Mr. Justice Romilly
writes:

[13]      The power
to make an order under s. 205 of the Company Act is a discretionary one. In
Kropp
v. Swaneset Bay Golf Course Ltd
. (1997),
1997 CanLII 4037 (BC CA)
, 29 B.C.L.R. (3d) 252 at 260-1
(B.C.C.A.), Finch J.A. set forth the principles that ought to guide the
exercise of that discretion:

The court has a
complete discretion whether to order security, and will act in light of all the
relevant circumstances; the possibility or probability that the plaintiff
company will be deterred from pursuing its claim is not, without more,
sufficient reason for not ordering security; the court must attempt to balance
injustices arising from use of security as an instrument of oppression to
stifle a legitimate claim on the one hand, and use of impecuniosity as a means
of putting unfair pressure on a defendant on the other; the court may have
regard to the merits of the action, but should avoid going into detail on the
merits unless success or failure appears obvious; the court can order any amount
of security up to the full amount claimed, as long as the amount is more than
nominal; before the court refuses to order security on the ground that it would
unfairly stifle a valid claim, the court must be satisfied that, in all the
circumstances, it is probable that the claim would be stifled; and the lateness
of the application for security is a circumstance which can properly be taken
into account.

[14]      Based
then, on the decision in
Kropp
, supra
as well as the decision of Spencer
J. in Ruko,
supra
, the test to be applied on an application for security
for costs is as follows:

1.         Does it appear
that the plaintiff company will be unable to pay the defendants' costs if the
action fails?

2.         If so, has the
plaintiff shown that it has exigible assets of sufficient value to satisfy an
award of costs?

3.         Is the court
satisfied that the defendants have an arguable defence to present?

4.         Would an order
for costs visit undue hardship on the plaintiff such that it would prevent the
plaintiff's case from being heard?

[
23
]

I have no problem concluding that it appears
that the plaintiff company will be unable to pay the defendant’s cost if the
action fails. I am also satisfied that the plaintiff has not shown that it has
exigible assets of sufficient value to satisfy an award of costs; its financial
statements demonstrate the contrary. The plaintiff did not submit that the
defendant did not have an arguable defence to present; on my review of the
pleadings there is an arguable defence.

[
24
]

Dealing with the undue hardship issue, Romilly
J., at paras. 22-23 writes as follows:

[22]      To succeed
in showing that an order for security would stifle the action, the plaintiff
must show that it has insufficient assets and no means of raising money for
security:
Kropp, supra
. In the case at bar, there is dearth evidence as
to the financial state of affairs of the plaintiff. There is also a dearth of
evidence as to any access the plaintiff may have to resources. Consequently,
though it appears that the plaintiff may be unable to pay costs of the action,
it does not follow, in the absence of evidence, that such a state of affairs
would result in stifling the advancement of the plaintiff's claim if costs were
ordered to be secured.

[23]      In sum, on an application for security for costs, once the
defendants have established a
prima facie
case that the plaintiff lacks
exigible assets, the plaintiff is required to respond with evidence to
establish either that it will be able to pay the defendants' costs, that the
defendants have no arguable case, or that an order for security will stifle the
action. These tests serve to balance the possible injustice of stifling the
corporate plaintiff's claim against the possible injustices of exposing the
defendants to a law suit where they could not recover their costs if
successful.

[
25
]

In
Kropp v. Swaneset Bay Golf Course Ltd.

(1997),
1997 CanLII 4037 (BC CA)
, 29 B.C.L.R. (3d) 252, Mr. Justice Finch, as he then was, sets out the
principles governing such an application as is before me, at para. 17:

[17]      In
Keary
Development v. Tarmac Construction
,
[1995] 3 All E.R. 534
, the English
Court of Appeal considered s. 726(1) of the
Companies Act
1985, reviewed
a number of authorities applying that provision or its predecessors, and then
set out the principles which emerged from those cases. The principles are
stated at pp. 539-542, and may be summarized in this way:

1.         The court has
a complete discretion whether to order security, and will act in light of all
the relevant circumstances;

2.         The
possibility or probability that the plaintiff company will be deterred from
pursuing its claim is not without more sufficient reason for not ordering
security;

3.         The court must
attempt to balance injustices arising from use of security as an instrument of
oppression to stifle a legitimate claim on the one hand, and use of
impecuniosity as a means of putting unfair pressure on a defendant on the
other;

4.         The court may
have regard to the merits of the action, but should avoid going into detail on
the merits unless success or failure appears obvious;

5.         The court can
order any amount of security up to the full amount claimed, as long as the
amount is more than nominal;

6.         Before the
court refuses to order security on the ground that it would unfairly stifle a
valid claim, the court must be satisfied that, in all the circumstances, it is
probable that the claim would be stifled; and

7.         The lateness
of the application for security is a circumstance which can properly be taken
into account.

[
26
]

Finch J.A. dealt with the issue of whether or
not an order for security will stifle the action at paras. 21-24:

[21]      In his
affidavit, Mr. Kropp said that he did "not have the resources to deposit
the amount sought by the defendants". The defendants claimed security for
costs and disbursements in the total sum of about $105,000. On the hearing of
the appeal, the defendants said an appropriate amount for future costs alone
would be about $95,000 and they were prepared to exclude from the claim
security for costs already incurred. Mr. Kropp did not provide any details in his
affidavit as to his own or the corporate plaintiff's lack of assets, or as to
the ability of either of them to sell assets, borrow money, or otherwise raise
funds sufficient to post reasonable security for costs.

[22]      To succeed
in showing that an order for security would stifle the action the plaintiff
must do more than show that it has no assets: see
Paul v. General Magnaplate
Corp
. (1995),
1995 CanLII 7259 (ON CTGD)
, 27 O.R. (3d) 314 (Gen.Div.). The defendants have already made
out a prima facie case that the corporate plaintiff has insufficient assets to
pay costs if unsuccessful. Mr. Kropp's affidavit does not really add to that
position and establish that the corporate plaintiff is impecunious, in the
sense of lacking any means of raising money for security. I think the law requires
him to do so. As Megarry, V.C., said in
Pearson, supra
, at 535, the
purpose of the provision is to protect "the community against litigious
abuses by artificial persons manipulated by natural persons."

[23]      Mr.
Kropp's affidavit provides only a blanket and empty assertion of impecuniosity.
In
Burke v. Larter
(1991),
1991 CanLII 13013 (PE SCAD)
, 305 A.P.R. 251 (P.E.I.C.A.), such an
assertion was rejected. The court at para.10 approved the decision of the
chambers judge who

held that the mere
assertion of impecuniosity is not sufficient to meet the test ... [and] that
plaintiffs who seek to avoid security for costs on the ground of impecuniosity
must lead evidence to demonstrate that they are impecunious by giving evidence
of their assets, debts, etc.

[24] So I am respectfully of the view that the learned chambers judge
erred in finding that the corporate plaintiff would be prevented from pursuing
its claim if security were to be ordered. And it would, in my view, be contrary
to the principles enunciated above to refuse security on the grounds that the
corporate plaintiff would "have difficulty" in pursuing the action if
security for costs were to be ordered. It seems likely, as the defendants
contend, that the learned chambers judge failed adequately to distinguish between
the position of Mr. Kropp as a natural person, and the corporate plaintiff as
an artifical legal entity. I think this is entirely understandable, given the
failure to distinguish in the statement of claim between the claims of the two
plaintiffs.

[
27
]

Those legal principles have been reaffirmed by
our Court of Appeal in
Ocean Pastures Corporation v. Old Masset Economic
Development Corporation
,
2016 BCCA 12
, a decision of Mr. Justice Goepel.

[
28
]

In
Seteri (Shanghai) Management Limited v.
Vinall
,
2013 BCSC 840
, Madam Justice Gropper gave judgment on an
application for security for costs. In her decision, she cited a decision of
Madam Justice Griffin in
Integrated Contractors Ltd
.
v. Leduc
Development Ltd.
,
2009 BCSC 965
. Paragraphs 14-15 of Griffin J’s decision,
cited at para. 8 of Gropper J’s decision, is as follows:

[14] In addition, there are other factors which may touch upon the
exercise of the court's discretion in determining whether or not to grant an
order requiring a party to post security for costs. Potentially relevant on the
facts of this application are the following factors:

a)         Where
the court is satisfied that ordering security for costs would unfairly stifle a
valid claim, the court may refuse to order security:
Kropp
at para.
17
;

b)         Where
the security for costs application is brought against a defendant advancing a
counterclaim, and the counterclaim is sufficiently intertwined with the
defendant's defence of the main claim:
Gray v. Powerassist Technologies Inc.
,

2001 BCSC 1208
, 10 C.P.C. (5th) 148 (B.C.S.C.), and
Scotford Electrical
& Technical Services Ltd. v. Blue Mountain Log Sales Ltd.
,
2005 BCSC
538
, 10 C.P.C. (6th) 237 (B.C.S.C., Master); and

c)         Where
the financial hardship that may give rise to the respondent's inability to pay
costs is due to the very actions of the applicants at issue in the respondent's
claim:
Tour-Mate Technologies Corp. v. Syntronix Systems Limited et al.
,

1993 CanLII 2250 (BC SC)
, [1993] B.C.J. No. 599 (S.C.); and
Middlekamp v. Fraser Valley Real Estate
Board
,
[1993] B.C.J. No. 2965 (S.C.)
.

[15]      Finally,
if the court concludes a security for costs order is warranted, the court has
discretion as to the quantum of security.

DISCUSSION AND DECISION

[
29
]

Donna Barnes’ affidavit attaches a draft bill of
costs at exhibit K, which sets out 360 units and estimates $18,000.00 in
disbursements, including $8,000.00 for expert fees.

[
30
]

Plaintiff’s counsel submits that this is not a
case where expert evidence will be needed, at least with respect to liability
issues. At this early stage, that is not entirely clear, but it does appear
that liability, at least, would probably not require opinion evidence.
Plaintiff’s counsel also submits that the liability issues at least could be
determined in much less than ten days.

[
31
]

Plaintiff’s counsel submits that many of the
units claimed are unlikely to be incurred. Tariff items dealing with
settlement, adjournment and mediation may not be incurred. The trial will
probably be about 10 days, but if liability is severed, the liability portion
will not take nearly that long.

[
32
]

Counsel for the plaintiff pointed out a number
of other items in the bill of costs which he submits would not likely be
incurred. He submits that this is one of those cases that may be amenable, at
least with respect to liability, to a Rule 9-7 application, perhaps with some
cross-examination. As an alternative submission, he says that if security for
costs is ordered, it should be a fraction of what is being sought.

[
33
]

I am mindful that there has been no affidavit
material emanating from the plaintiff to the effect that its claim will be
stifled. The principals of the plaintiff may well have some ability to pay
costs; they have not filed affidavit material to the contrary.

[
34
]

On the other hand, as set out by Griffin J. in
Integrated
Contractors Ltd
